Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: This strategy is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The trigger, threat, and memory items all center on intrusive reliving, bodily/sensory cues, and generalized danger/safety monitoring after terrorism, but nothing else points specifically to vehicles or transport-related threat. For a terrorism trauma this is possible, but without any corresponding trigger, memory, or threat content linked to cars/roads/passenger situations, this item stands out as a likely incoherent addition rather than part of the same formulation.

vignette: María, a 44‑year‑old nun in a small California convent, had spent the last decade tending to a Catholic school and praying in the parish. In her early twenties, while standing beside the altar during a community Mass, a sudden explosion shattered the peace of the nave. The blast sent shards of glass and a spray of blood across the pews; the crowd erupted in screams. The pain that lingered in the back of her neck, the flash of crimson on the church floor, and the echoing roar of that day became the raw material of her memories. The night after the attack, María woke repeatedly from a nightmare of fire and blood, the dream residue pressing her back into a state of dread. The vividness of that trauma meant that even a sudden physical ache in her lower back could bring the scene back to life, as if the memory had leapt out of the past and into her present. The visceral pain María felt when she tightened her shoulders to lift a crate during a routine stocking of the convent pantry triggered an immediate surge of negative emotions—fear, horror, and a deep shame that something so horrific had happened in a place she believed should be safe. The sight of a stranger’s bloodstained sleeve in a crowded market outside the church further amplified those emotions. In each instance, the pain and the visual cue of blood served as a trigger that pulled her straight into the throes of that terror, turning the ordinary into a stark reminder of her vulnerability. The emotional surge that followed was not merely a reaction; it intensified her perception of threat and made the moment feel overwhelmingly perilous. When the memory of the bombing burst into María’s consciousness, it did so in a full sensory reliving: the metallic taste of blood, the sharp crack of shattering glass, the oppressive heat of the fire that had followed the explosion. This uncontrolled access forced her to overanalyze the details, retracing the positions of people, the exact moment the bomb detonated, the route the smoke had taken. Over time, this overanalysis became a maladaptive strategy, a way to make sense of an event that refused to stay still. The memory’s return also flooded María with a sense of threat—her body was suddenly flooded with fear and guilt. Because she felt that safety existed only in a narrow circle—the convent’s quiet rooms and the familiar chapel—she began planning escape routes each time she felt a hint of danger. The constant planning and avoidance of crowds kept her in a perpetual state of vigilance, ensuring that the threat was never truly left behind. The more María avoided intimate contact, the less she could share the weight of her fears with others. Each avoidance of close conversations with fellow sisters or students reinforced her belief that she alone should bear the memory of the attack. Her avoidance also magnified the threat she sensed; the isolation made her feel more exposed, as if the threat could strike without any one to offer support. The cycle tightened: each escape route she mapped out, each time she stayed away from the bustling Sunday services, was both a response to and a reinforcement of the threat she felt. The pain in her body, the blood in the world around her, the memories that came unbidden—all these elements kept María in a loop that seemed impossible to break. Now, after months of growing anxiety that made even the routine tasks of her convent feel like potential disaster sites, María has come to her therapist with a clear sense of fear: she fears that a single moment—a sudden ache, a bright flash of color, an unfamiliar crowd—will again summon the terror of that day. Her hope, however, lies in learning whether she can move beyond the need to overanalyze, to find a place where she feels truly safe, and to reconnect with others without feeling that any intimacy will betray her fragile sense of security.
